stories.headline: IAF has evolved into exceptional, network-centric force: Air Chief Marshal A P Singh
stories.title: IAF has evolved into exceptional, network-centric force: Air Chief Marshal A P Singh
stories.summary: Ghaziabad (UP), Oct 8: Since its inception in 1932, the IAF has evolved into an exceptional, capable, network-centric and multi-domain force that is alert and ready to meet any contingency, Chief of the Air Staff Air Chief Marshal A P Singh said on Thursday. In his address at the Air Force Day celebrations at the Hindan air base here, the IAF chief also said conflicts in parts of the world have shown that air power is the primary means of protecting the national interest. Referring to Operation Sindoor, he said the Indian Air Force (IAF) showed "speed of combat operations" with both its precision strike and air defence capabilities. Air Force Day is observed on October 8 to commemorate the establishment of the force and the sacrifices made by air warriors. The IAF chief also said "success in modern conflict demands deep synergy" and that joint planning and integrated combat application with the Army and Navy is a daily activity. Navy Chief Admiral Krishna Swaminathan and Army Chief Gen Dhiraj Seth and other senior military officials were also present at the event. Several former IAF chiefs were also in attendance. Air Chief Marshal Singh credited the air warriors with lending strength to the IAF, and said the force is alert, committed and ready to meet any challenges. "Our operational capabilities are growing in the right direction," he said, adding that the force would leave no stone unturned to live up to expectations, rather exceed them. The IAF chief said an air force can have the most advanced aircraft in the world, but its true strength is measured by its operational preparedness -- "how quickly and confidently it can act whenever the call comes". He underlined that 'Infallible, Impervious, Precise' is not just a tagline, "it is the manifestation of our strength and resolve". He recalled the proud legacy of the IAF and urged it to remain an agile and combat-ready force. "From four Wapiti aircraft, the force has evolved into an exceptional, capable, network-centric and multi-domain force ranked among the finest in the world," he said. According to the IAF website, the force's initial "aircraft inventory consisted of four Westland Wapiti IIA army co-operation biplanes at Drigh Road as the 'A' Flight nucleus of the planned No.1 (Army Co-operation) Squadron". Today, the IAF has 29 fighter squadrons. On his superannuation on October 31, Air Chief Marshal Singh said serving as the IAF chief was "my biggest fortune" and it was a proud moment for him. Air Marshal Ashutosh Dixit will be the next Chief of Air Staff. The IAF marked the 94th anniversary of its establishment with a ceremonial parade, a static display of some of its prized combat assets such as Rafale and Tejas and a flypast by three Mi-17 helicopters. Aerial manoeuvres by a British-era Tiger Moth drew loud cheers from the audience. Air Chief Marshal Singh arrived at the parade venue in a 1960s-era car, with the three helicopters in 'Dhwaj' formation flying past him. The creamy white left hand-drive car carries the plate number "IAF 1". An IAF drum band made its parade debut, while 'Team Shakti', a group of women air warriors who performed skilful drills with rifles, also won the appreciation of the audience. The IAF Drummers Team, comprising 33 young air warriors, presented a vibrant display featuring snare drums, roto drums, bass drums and cymbals, accompanied by dynamic formations and acrobatic movements, officials said. The theme for this year's Air Force Day was 'Indian Air Force: Infallible, Impervious and Precise', reflecting the IAF's unwavering commitment to safeguard the nation's skies with precision, resilience and operational excellence. The IAF also put on display on the tarmac fighter jets such as Su-30 MKI, Jaguar; helicopters such as LCH Prachand and ALH Dhruv; and critical weapon and air defence systems such as BrahMos and Akash, Rohini radar system and a Dornier aircraft. The parade was commanded by Gp Capt Manish Sharma and was followed by an investiture ceremony, during which various air warriors were awarded medals for gallantry and distinguished service. Unit citations were also presented to various units for excellence. Five unit citations were presented to 24 Squadron -- 'The Hawks', 110 Helicopter Unit -- 'The Vanguards', 200 Squadron -- 'Skanda', 2402 Squadron -- 'Vajra', and the Electronic Warfare Range, the defence ministry said in a statement. Sqn No. 24 (The Hawks), which saw "considerable action" during the India-Pakistan War of 1965, also received a unit citation on Thursday, a senior official said. The Hawks was raised at Air Force Station Chabua in Assam in 1962. From Gnat to MiG-21, followed by Su-30K and ultimately Su-30MKI, it has reinvented itself with evolution of India's air power, the officials said. Following the celebrations at Hindan air base, the Air Force Day aerial display will be conducted at Namo Ghat, Varanasi, on October 25, officials said. Reiterating the IAF's commitment to technological advancement and self-reliance, the air chief marshal said, "Atmanirbharta is our guiding principle", and emphasised that emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence and autonomous systems, would be integrated while keeping human authority at the core. Space is a natural extension of air domain, he said, and highlighted the growing collaboration with ISRO and domestic space industry, including the IAF's role in the Gaganyaan human spaceflight mission.

stories.headline: Explosions are heard in Saudi capital as Riyadh airport is reported closed
stories.title: Explosions are heard in Saudi capital as Riyadh airport is reported closed
stories.summary: Cairo, Oct 8: Several explosions were heard in Saudi Arabia's capital of Riyadh on Thursday, including a large blast at the city's international airport, a witness told The Associated Press, a day after the kingdom said an attack there killed one person and wounded others. The cause of the blasts was not immediately known. There was no immediate claim of responsibility. Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen have repeatedly claimed attacks against airports, military and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia in recent days. The blasts had an immediate effect on markets and oil prices as the price of crude jumped. King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh “closed again,” the Flightradar24 monitor said Thursday on X. “Last landing 80+ minutes ago. Last take off 90+ minutes ago.” Fire and ambulance crews were deployed and smoke was visible, the witness said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media. The witness said outgoing flights were halted and passengers were instructed to leave all checked-in luggage behind and evacuate the airport. It was not immediately clear how many flights were disrupted. Saudi authorities did not respond to requests for comment. On Wednesday, Saudi officials said two attacks on airports claimed by the Houthis had killed three people, as the kingdom was pulled deeper into the latest front in the Iran war. The attack on King Khalid airport killed a Sudanese national and wounded eight other people, and the attack on Abha airport killed Moroccan and Algerian residents and wounded 28 others, officials said. Attacks on the kingdom, the world's top oil exporter, have raised alarm. Over the weekend, Saudi Arabia and allied Yemeni forces launched a major ground and air offensive aimed at retaking territory that the Houthis seized a month ago along Yemen's western Red Sea coast and on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The rebels' presence on the waterway poses a threat to the crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where traffic has been curtailed due to the Iran war. Also Wednesday, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, said forces destroyed a platform in Yemen's rebel-held capital of Sanaa that had been used to launch attacks on the Saudi capital. The AP could not independently verify these claims. (AP)

stories.headline: Microfinance's reckoning: Can India's lenders grow without repeating the past?
stories.title: Microfinance's reckoning: Can India's lenders grow without repeating the past?
stories.summary: For years, India's microfinance industry ran on the formula of lending small amounts to millions of low-income households, keeping collections high, adding borrowers and branches and letting scale do the rest. The model made microfinance one of the country's most important channels of formal credit for households conventional banks found too expensive to serve.After surviving the Covid-19 pandemic, the industry entered the post-pandemic period with confidence. Demand returned strongly, capital was plentiful, new players entered and competition for borrowers intensified. “Microfinance institutions were mono-line businesses for a long time due to regulatory prescription," says Ganesh Narayanan, CEO and MD of CreditAccess Grameen. The problem was not just an external shock hitting an otherwise sound business; it was perhaps the first time, the sector itself had begun to overheat.Lenders competed for customers already borrowing from several institutions, and indebtedness accumulated beneath what still looked like healthy growth. At the peak, around a quarter of CreditAccess Grameen's AUM was linked to borrowers with exposure to more than three lenders; that figure is now around 2 percent.The warning signs were visible in credit-bureau data, but the industry was slow to act. When collections deteriorated in 2024, the first explanations were external—heat waves, elections, campaigns against indebtedness.Then came the Karza Mukti Abhiyan and legislative intervention, most notably in Karnataka. What looked like temporary disturbances exposed a deeper vulnerability: Credit had grown faster than the industry's ability to assess a household's total repayment capacity. However, not all credit stress is the same. A borrower hit by a drought can recover once the shock passes; a household that has taken on debt beyond what it can service faces a different problem entirely.The industry spent much of the downturn figuring out which it was dealing with. By the time leverage emerged as the bigger issue, lenders were already facing higher credit costs, weaker collections, tighter funding and a sceptical investor base.In response, underwriting tightened, scrutiny of household indebtedness increased, and borrower-level monitoring strengthened. By mid-2026, around 98 percent of borrowers were within the industry's lender-count limits meaning no borrower can borrow from more than three lenders.ICRA reports a meaningful reduction in overleveraging—95 percent of borrowers now have exposure to three lenders or fewer. It expects assets under management growth to rebound to 15-17 per cent in FY27. But with cleaner credit metrics, can these businesses generate attractive returns without eventually recreating the same problem?With a bit of caution in mind, Gautam Trivedi, co-founder and managing partner at Nepean Capital, says, "We will stay away from these stocks.” In his view, some of the industry's difficulties are structural rather than cyclical—borrowers stacking multiple loans, weak enforceability, and the risk of legislative intervention, like Karnataka showed.Also Read: How No-Cost-EMIs have changed the way Indians shopBorrowers Still ExistIndia's low-income households still need working capital, emergency finance, and money for housing and small businesses.Moneylenders still operate alongside formal institutions, proof that demand in this segment far exceeds what the formal MFI industry serves. Venkatesh Krishnan, CEO of Spandana Sphoorty, believes this is why microfinance will remain relevant for decades. What has changed is the borrower. A customer who enters the system with a Rs 30,000 joint-liability loan won't stay a microfinance customer forever.As income and business needs grow, so does demand. For the lender, instead of constantly acquiring new borrowers, it can retain the ones it already knows and grow the relationship.The scale of that opportunity shows at CreditAccess Grameen. Its existing customers have borrowed roughly Rs 83,000 crore from other lenders while its own "graduation" portfolio—where customers borrow outside of microfinance—is only around Rs 5,600 crore as of June 2026.This implies that the industry's future may lie less in finding millions of new borrowers than in following existing customers as their needs evolve. That's a reshaping strategy, rather than staying pure-play joint-liability lenders, MFIs want to become broader financial-services companies serving the same customer across life stages.Regulation has helped too. In June 2025, the RBI cut the qualifying-asset requirement for NBFC-MFIs from 75 percent to 60 percent of total assets, giving them room to diversify. This means that lenders can now have 40 percent of their loans outside microfinance compared to 25 percent earlier.CreditAccess Grameen wants roughly half its business from non-MFI activities by 2031, with 20-30 percent of its portfolio in secured loans. Spandana is keeping joint-liability lending as its core while expanding individual loans and loans against property.Across the sector, lenders are talking about migrating customers to secured products and using data to spot borrowers capable of larger loans. The challenge is distinguishing a borrower whose income has genuinely grown from one whose apparent capacity simply reflects more debt. That may be the central lesson of the downturn: growth alone is no longer enough.Also Read: Why retailers love buy now, pay laterThe Economics Have To ChangeThe real test now isn't whether loan growth returns. It’s whether lenders can grow while producing acceptable returns through an entire credit cycle, a much higher bar than before.The numbers offer a sobering baseline. According to Alok Misra, CEO of the Micro Finance Industry Network (MFIN), the top 15 microfinance companies generated average ROA of about 2.2 percent and ROE of roughly 8.5 percent between 2016 and 2024—a period that includes Covid's disruption.MFIN believes a well-run microfinance business should generate around 3.5 percent ROA and 15-16 percent return on equity over a cycle. Returns of 20-22 percent, while possible in good years, are unlikely to be sustainable without taking on more risk.That creates a balancing act. The strongest players have spent years building distribution networks and field forces that are valuable but operationally heavy.With pricing competitive and credit costs still elevated, margin is limited, and charging borrowers more isn't really an option. Even though pricing has been deregulated, it stays politically sensitive. The more durable path is improving productivity, using technology better, and deepening each customer relationship—which is where diversification comes in.The RBI's June 2025 rule change lets lenders hold up to 40 percent of their books outside microfinance, effectively turning microfinance into a customer-acquisition engine rather than the whole business.Gold loans, individual loans, housing finance and MSME lending offer larger ticket sizes and different risk profiles, reducing the earnings volatility of relying almost entirely on unsecured group lending.For bigger players, even a modest slice of a large balance sheet can be meaningful. CreditAccess Grameen's historical ROA has swung between 4-5 percent in good years and 1-2 percent in bad ones; the ambition behind its diversification push is a more consistent cross-cycle 4 percent.Another lesson that may matter as much as diversification is that the industry needs to know exactly who it's lending to. The multiple-lending problem was partly a failure of borrower identification."The need for a unique identifier is very important," says Baskar Babu R, MD of Suryoday Small Finance Bank. The industry is moving towards PAN and CKYC as the only acceptable borrower identifiers.The Road AheadFunding may determine which lenders emerge strongest. The crisis exposed a clear divide between institutions with strong balance sheets and smaller players that struggled to raise money.A government-backed Rs 20,000 crore credit guarantee scheme has helped. Industry estimates suggest around Rs 450 crore of funding has been facilitated for 25-30 smaller institutions. It doesn't solve the funding problem outright, but it gives banks more comfort at a time when their appetite for MFI exposure has fallen.That imbalance could accelerate consolidation, as smaller MFIs decide whether to raise expensive capital, sell, or become business correspondents for larger lenders. But similar predictions were made during earlier funding crises, and pure-play MFIs didn't disappear then either. As of July, NBFC-MFIs accounted for about 45 percent of the market as per MFIN data, against 23 percent for banks.Even if every MFI follows its guardrails, the same customer can still borrow from a fintech, NBFC or bank outside the MFI framework, or from informal lenders outside the bureau system entirely and this remains an unsolved problem. That's why a unique identifier and cross-lender coordination matter as much as any single lender's discipline.Political risk is the other uncomfortable variable. The past two years showed how quickly borrower distress can turn political, and how a state government's intervention can reshape an entire industry's operating environment, a key reason for scepticism like Trivedi's."The learnings of this crisis will stay for long," says Babu. If memories fade as growth accelerates, the next cycle could resemble the last one. Meanwhile, for investors, proof will come through numbers, not promises—credit costs normalising, ROE moving toward sustainable levels, and growth returning without another rise in borrower leverage.

stories.headline: CAPF Act that governs officer posts, deputation comes into force
stories.title: CAPF Act that governs officer posts, deputation comes into force
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 8: The Central Armed Police Forces (General Administration) Act, 2026, which provides a common framework for recruitment and conditions of service of Group-A general duty officers and other officers in the CAPFs, came into force on Thursday, according a government notification. The notification came at a time when the Supreme Court is hearing a bunch of petitions filed by thousands of CAPF officers challenging the validity of the law that was passed by the Parliament in April. "In exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (2) of section 1 of the Central Armed Police Forces (General Administration) Act, 2026, the Central Government hereby appoints the 08th day of October, 2026, as the date on which the provisions of the said Act shall come into force," said the notification issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs. The CAPF Act provides for regulation of recruitment, promotion, deputation and other conditions of service of officers in the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), Border Security Force (BSF), Central Industrial Security Force (CISF), Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) and Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB). The Centre recently told the apex court through an affidavit that the appointment of Group 'A' general duty officers in the respective CAPFs is now regulated by the CAPF (General Administration) Act. It had said that the Act "expressly empowers" the Central government to prescribe the method, manner and mode of recruitment, including by deputation, and the conditions of service of officers in the five CAPFs-- CRPF, BSF, CISF, ITBP and SSB. The cadre officers of these forces have petitioned the top court, including by filing a contempt petition, that the Act continues to restrict their career progression in comparison to the Indian Police Service (IPS) officers brought on deputation. They have also asked the apex court to direct the Union government to implement its May 2025 judgement that said that the deputation of IPS officers up to the rank of inspector general in the CAPFs should be "progressively reduced" over a period of two years in order to give more opportunities to cadre officers whose delayed promotions can "adversely" impact the morale of these forces. Under the new legislation, 50 per cent of the posts in the rank of inspector general are to be filled through deputation from the IPS, while a minimum of 67 per cent of posts at the additional director general level are to be filled through deputation. The posts in the ranks of special director general and director general are to be filled through deputation only. The Act comes against the backdrop of the Supreme Court's May 2025 judgment on the deputation of IPS officers in the CAPFs. In October last year, the apex court dismissed the Centre’s plea seeking a review of its 2025 verdict. The court had said the number of posts earmarked for deputation in CAPF cadres up to the SAG level should be progressively reduced over a period of time, with an outer limit of two years, and had directed a cadre review. The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the legislation said the expanding functional and operational requirements of the CAPFs had resulted in a distinct organisational structure for the forces. "In recent years, due to the absence of an umbrella law, regulatory provisions have evolved in a fragmented manner, resulting in several litigation on service-related matters, leading to some functional and administrative difficulties," it said. The law replaces the fragmented framework governing service matters with a common legislative framework for Group-A general duty officers and other officers in the five CAPFs. A group of retired CAPF officers had also approached the Supreme Court with a contempt plea against then Home Secretary Govind Mohan over alleged non-implementation of the apex court's October 2025 order. The group had said any legislative intervention affecting the command structure, service conditions and leadership opportunities within the CAPFs would have implications for institutional morale and the operational effectiveness of forces responsible for internal security and border security.

stories.headline: Police register FIR to probe violence during CJP's July 20 protest
stories.title: Police register FIR to probe violence during CJP's July 20 protest
stories.summary: The Crime Branch of the Delhi Police has registered an FIR to investigate the violence that broke out during the Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) protest in the national capital on July 20, police sources said on Thursday. The probe will focus on identifying people allegedly responsible for the violence and examine whether it was premeditated, the sources said. On the directions of the Supreme Court, the Delhi Police had cancelled 17 FIRs registered at multiple police stations in the New Delhi district. The FIR comes two days ahead of another CJP protest announced to be held at Jantar Mantar, this time to press for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the SIR exercise. A police officer said that permission has not been granted for any protest. Referring to the fresh FIR, the police source told PTI that teams of the Crime Branch will also look into whether criminal elements entered the protest sites after the CJP called for a march

stories.headline: Supreme Court expands scrutiny of DGP appointment laws nationwide after Jharkhand questions Centre’s ‘special affection’
stories.title: Supreme Court expands scrutiny of DGP appointment laws nationwide after Jharkhand questions Centre’s ‘special affection’
stories.summary: Court requests its amicus curiae, senior advocate Raju Ramachandran, to take the help of the Union Public Service Commission and scrutinise police laws and DGP appointments nationwide for breaches of the 2006 verdict
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: Jharkhand’s Hemant Soren government locked horns with the Centre in the Supreme Court on Thursday (October 8, 2026) over the appointment of Directors General of Police (DGPs), calling out the Union government’s “special affection” for the State when others like Bihar had “worse” appointment laws.
The confrontation erupted after the Union government moved the court against Jharkhand’s 2025 law governing the appointment of DGPs.

Appearing before a three-judge Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, for the Centre, sought a judicial declaration that the ‘Selection and Appointment of Director General and Inspector General of Police, Jharkhand (Head of Police), Regulation of 2025’ breached the apex court’s 2006 judgment in Prakash Singh versus Union of India.
The 2006 judgment had mandated insulation of the police force from political influence.
It laid down a transparent DGP appointment process followed by a minimum tenure of two years in office.
Only senior police officers with a residual tenure of six months before normal retirement could be considered for the top post.

To ensure timely compliance, State governments were directed to submit service credentials of eligible IPS officers to the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) at least three months before an incumbent’s retirement.
The Centre contended that the appointment of Jharkhand’s first woman DGP and incumbent Tadasha Mishra under the 2025 Regulation violated the Prakash Singh verdict.
Observing that the 2025 Regulation appeared prima facie non-compliant, the Bench observed that the flaw could imperil Ms. Mishra’s tenure.
However, the Bench granted Ms. Mishra an opportunity to state her case on November 3, the next date of hearing.
At this juncture, senior advocate Kapil Sibal, for Jharkhand, turned the tables on the Centre by asking why it had no similar complaints about other States.
He highlighted that West Bengal’s DGP was appointed by the Election Commission of India in March 2026 even though the officer was due to retire the next month.

stories.headline: Elon Musk again stirs the Starlink India pot
stories.title: Elon Musk again stirs the Starlink India pot
stories.summary: Elon Musk on Thursday questioned why Starlink is yet to receive a licence to operate in India, saying the satellite internet company has spent five years complying with the country’s laws and government requirements.“Starlink is licensed in over 165 countries and has spent five years complying with every single law and requirement of the government of India, so why still no license?” Musk said in a post on X.Also read: Musk pitches Starlink for India's no-internet, no-network areas a day after 'oligarchs' charge— elonmusk (@elonmusk) The remarks come a day after the SpaceX founder accused unnamed “oligarchs” of blocking Starlink’s entry into India to protect their business interests.Unfortunately, we are being blocked by certain oligarchs in order to maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people,” Musk had said on Wednesday. “You can guess who they are … This is a crime against the people of India!”Starlink awaits final approvalsStarlink has secured a satellite communication permit and authorisation from India’s space regulator, but is still awaiting a security clearance from the government before it can begin commercial services.The company is not alone in waiting for the final approvals. Bharti Group-backed Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio Satellite also have the required satcom permit and space-sector authorisation but are awaiting security clearance. The companies also need spectrum to launch commercial services, with the government expected to take a decision on spectrum pricing.At the India Mobile Congress on Wednesday, SpaceX vice president for Starlink business operations Lauren Dreyer said the company had built 20 gateway sites and hundreds of antennas in India and had adapted its operations to meet Indian security and regulatory requirements, including keeping Indian user data within the country.“We built our Starlink operations specifically for India in recognition of Indian security requirements and other regulations, establishing controls of every layer for India, and keeping Indian user data within India,” Dreyer said.She said Starlink had spent five years working with Indian regulators, industry and telecom operators to prepare for its entry into the Indian market.Also read: Elon Musk says Starlink's entry in India 'blocked' by oligarchs, alleges 'monopolistic chokehold'Musk presses India on Starlink entryDreyer said Starlink’s management was in regular contact with authorities to resolve outstanding issues and that the company was ready to begin operations once approvals were completed.“Hopefully, next time I address the Congress, the government’s good work will have been complete and Starlink will be authorised and ready and reporting on stories here,” she said. “We’re ready to work with the government, ready to work with operators, ready to work with industry to this end.”Starlink has also signed letters of intent with the state governments of Maharashtra and Meghalaya to explore connectivity for remote communities and public institutions.In March 2025, Starlink signed agreements with Bharti Airtel and Reliance Jio covering network equipment distribution, business connectivity and rural connectivity.Dreyer said the company was seeking to work with Indian telecom operators and state governments as it prepared for a commercial launch.

Bharti Group-backed Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio Satellite also have the required satcom permit and space-sector authorisation but are awaiting security clearance.
